content: Children with diarrhea should be assessed for dehydration severity using clinical signs. Pinching the skin on the abdomen to test for decreased skin turgor is a common method. Dehydration is classified into three categories: severe dehydration, some dehydration, and no dehydration. Severe Dehydration: Diagnosis: Severe dehydration is diagnosed if a child with diarrhea exhibits two or more of the following signs: Lethargy or unconsciousness Sunken eyes Inability to drink or drinking poorly Skin pinch that returns very slowly (≥2 seconds) Treatment: Immediate intravenous (IV) rehydration is required. While setting up the IV, oral rehydration solution (ORS) can be given if the child is able to drink. Administer 100 mL/kg of the chosen IV solution over a specified period. Avoid hypotonic solutions like 0.18% saline with 5% dextrose to prevent hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Reassess hydration status every 15–30 minutes until a strong radial pulse is present. After IV rehydration, switch to oral rehydration therapy and zinc supplementation. In areas with cholera outbreaks, provide an effective antibiotic against cholera strains. Persistent severe dehydration after IV therapy is rare and may indicate ongoing large-volume watery stools. Some Dehydration: Diagnosis: Some dehydration is diagnosed if a child with diarrhea shows two or more of the following signs: Restlessness or irritability Sunken eyes Drinking eagerly or being very thirsty Skin pinch that returns slowly Treatment: Administer ORS solution based on the child’s weight or age over the first 4 hours. Teach the caregiver how to prepare and give ORS. Monitor the child during this period and reassess after 4 hours. If dehydration persists, repeat ORS treatment and begin feeding. Zinc supplementation should also be initiated. If the child is breastfeeding, encourage frequent breastfeeding. If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and continue ORS more slowly. No Dehydration: Diagnosis: No dehydration is diagnosed if the child does not exhibit two or more signs of dehydration. Treatment: Provide extra fluids at home to prevent dehydration. Continue an appropriate diet for the child’s age, including breastfeeding. Teach the caregiver the four rules of home treatment: 1. Give extra fluids. 2. Continue feeding. 3. Administer zinc supplements. 4. Know when to return to the clinic (e.g., if the child becomes sicker, develops fever, or has blood in the stool). Zinc Supplementation: Zinc is essential for recovery and reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea episodes. It also lowers the risk of future diarrhea within 2–3 months. Dosage: Children ≤6 months: 10 mg (half tablet) daily for 10–14 days. Children >6 months: 20 mg (one tablet) daily for 10–14 days. For infants, dissolve the tablet in clean water, expressed breast milk, or ORS. Older children can chew the tablet or drink it dissolved. Feeding During Diarrhea: Continue breastfeeding frequently throughout the diarrhea episode. If the child cannot suckle, provide expressed breast milk orally or via a nasogastric tube. After the initial 4-hour rehydration period, introduce food every 3–4 hours if dehydration persists. For children >6 months, provide freshly prepared, age-appropriate foods such as mashed or ground foods, cooked meals, and potassium-rich options like mashed bananas or fresh fruit juice. Encourage the child to eat at least six times a day and provide an extra meal daily for two weeks after diarrhea stops. Persistent Diarrhea: Persistent diarrhea lasts ≥14 days and may or may not involve blood. If dehydration is present, classify it as severe. Children with persistent diarrhea but no severe malnutrition should be managed with appropriate hydration and nutritional support. In areas with high HIV prevalence, assess for HIV infection if other suggestive clinical signs are present. Monitoring and Follow-Up: Reassess hydration status regularly during treatment. For severe dehydration, monitor every 15–30 minutes initially, then hourly. For some dehydration, reassess after 4 hours. If the child is not improving, adjust the treatment plan or refer to a hospital. Advise caregivers to return immediately if the child becomes sicker, is unable to drink or breastfeed, develops fever, or has blood in the stool. If the child is not improving but shows no danger signs, follow up after 5 days. Home Care Instructions: Teach caregivers how to prepare and administer ORS. Provide enough ORS packets for rehydration and two additional days. Encourage continued breastfeeding and appropriate feeding practices. Explain the importance of zinc supplementation and ensure the caregiver understands the dosage and duration. By following these guidelines, dehydration and diarrhea can be effectively managed, reducing complications and improving outcomes for affected children.
